Rating: Active Researcher (40.2/100) Basic Metrics Metric Value Institution Unknown h-index 12 Total Citations 451 Recent 5 Years Citations 174 Total Papers 23 Papers in Top Conferences 0 Publication Period 2005 - 2023 Semantic Scholar 46522031 Research Trajectory It should be noted first: there is a clear name disambiguation issue in this paper list. The papers span completely unrelated fields such as cancer biology, GPU architecture, plant immunity, hyperspectral image processing, genomics, and LLM prompt engineering. Clearly, they originate from the aggregation of multiple researchers with the same name. Based on publication years, citation counts, and thematic coherence, at least 3 different Xiaoxiao Liu can be identified: (1) in the field of molecular oncology (contributing most of the 451 citations, including the highest-cited paper on miR-1271 pancreatic cancer with 62 citations and papers at the level of Nature Communications/JEM/PNAS); (2) in computer architecture/image processing (GPU memory design, hyperspectral denoising); (3) in LLM/AI safety (prompt engineering and safety evaluation from 2023–2025). The following analysis mainly focuses on the most representative and best-documented molecular oncology researcher, whose research trajectory shows a gradual progression from microRNA regulation → p53-MDM2 targeted therapy → E3 ubiquitin ligase tumor suppression → CHIP clonal hematopoiesis.
Breakthrough Work 1. miR-1271 inhibits migration, invasion, and epithelial-mesenchymal transition by targeting ZEB1 and TWIST1 in pancreatic cancer cells (2016) Description: For the first time, it systematically elucidated that miR-1271 suppresses the migration, invasion, and epithelial-mesenchymal transition of pancreatic cancer cells by simultaneously targeting two core EMT transcription factors, ZEB1 and TWIST1, providing a dual-target miRNA regulatory framework for the metastasis mechanism of pancreatic cancer.
Why it couldn’t be done before: Before 2016, the cost of high-throughput sequencing of miRNAs was too high, and systematic studies on the miRNA regulatory networks in pancreatic cancer were limited; the mechanism by which ZEB1 and TWIST1 were co-targeted by the same miRNA had not been revealed. Only with the popularization of NGS technology and the maturity of bioinformatics analysis tools was it possible to systematically screen and verify this dual-target regulatory axis.
Impact: The paper with 62 citations, which is the highest-cited paper by this researcher, promoted the establishment of multi-target miRNA regulatory strategies in pancreatic cancer metastasis research and has important reference value for subsequent studies on EMT-related therapeutic targets.
2. Antitumor immunity enhances the therapeutic effects of p53 activation on acute myeloid leukemia (2019) Description: Published in Nature Communications, it demonstrated that the oral active p53-MDM2 interaction inhibitor DS-5272 not only exerts antitumor effects by directly activating the p53 signal in AML cells but also synergizes with the host’s antitumor immune response, revealing the synergistic mechanism between targeted therapy and tumor immunity.
Why it couldn’t be done before: p53-MDM2 inhibitors were long considered to act through cellular autonomous pathways, and the long-standing separation between oncology and targeted drug research made it difficult to discover this synergy. Around 2019, the integration of immun oncology and small molecule targeted therapy became a research hotspot. The maturity of single-cell typing technologies such as CyTOF (with supporting datasets published in the same year) made it possible to accurately quantify the dynamic changes in immune cell subsets.
Impact: Published in Nature Communications with 42 citations, it expanded p53-targeted therapy research in AML from a single cell killing paradigm to the immune regulatory dimension, providing a theoretical basis for the design of clinical combination immune checkpoint inhibitor regimens later on.
3. Mutational inactivation of mTORC1 repressor gene DEPDC5 in human gastrointestinal stromal tumors (2019) Description: Published in PNAS, it reported for the first time that mutation-induced inactivation of the mTORC1 negative regulatory gene DEPDC5 is an important driver of GIST progression (rather than initiation), and clarified a new molecular mechanism for the malignant progression of GIST after KIT/PDGFRA mutations.
Why it couldn’t be done before: DEPDC5 had been mainly studied in neurological diseases (such as focal epilepsy), and its association with GIST had not been discovered for a long time. Research on the progression mechanism of GIST requires large-scale genomic sequencing data; the large-scale application of next-generation sequencing in clinical tumor samples, combined with a systematic research design on the evolutionary trajectory of ‘micro-GIST→progressing GIST’, is a prerequisite for this discovery.
Impact: Published with 34 citations, it provided a new explanation for the progression mechanism after GIST targeted therapy resistance, and the mTOR pathway entered the candidate list of GIST treatment targets, having direct clinical translation value.
4. E3 ligase MKRN3 is a tumor suppressor regulating PABPC1 ubiquitination in non–small cell lung cancer (2021) Description: Published in Journal of Experimental Medicine, it found that the pathogenic gene MKRN3 for central precocious puberty is a true tumor suppressor in NSCLC, and it regulates global protein synthesis through targeting PABPC1 ubiquitination modification, revealing a completely new ‘E3 ligase-mRNA-binding protein-proteome homeostasis’ tumor suppression axis.
Why it couldn’t be done before: MKRN3 was previously recognized only as a developmental regulation gene, and its function in tumors was completely unknown. This discovery required a unique perspective of cross-referencing clinical genetics of central precocious puberty with cancer genomics databases, as well as mature ubiquitomics protein profiling techniques to identify PABPC1 as a substrate. This cognitive leap from ‘endocrine disease gene→tumor suppressor’ depends on the completeness of large-scale cancer genome maps (such as TCGA) databases.
Impact: Published with 41 citations, it provided a new tumor suppression mechanism and potential therapeutic targets for NSCLC, while also creating a new paradigm for studying ‘reuse of developmental genes in tumors’.
5. The first phase (1996—2004) focused on the petroleum engineering field, concentrating on gas reservoir condensate prediction, CO₂ injection for enhanced oil recovery (EOR), and gas injection reservoir screening evaluation, with a clear background in Chinese oil fields (Liaohe, Daqing, etc.). The second phase (2005—2011) shifted significantly to geotechnical and civil engineering, with publications such as finite element analysis of dam stability, flood dikes in Louisiana, and pile foundation testing in Georgia—characteristic of North American engineering projects—with almost no connection to petroleum engineering. The third phase (2017—2019) returned to the petroleum field, but the research level was elevated to rock physics and unconventional reservoir mechanisms—focusing on compaction of unconsolidated sandstone, the impact of sand production on flow, and NMR spontaneous imbibition in tight sandstone, reflecting the large-scale development of shale oil/tight oil in China. The most cited paper (2019, 108 citations) represents the peak of his academic influence.
Breakthrough Works 1. New insights into spontaneous imbibition in tight oil sandstones with NMR (2019) Description: Using nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) technology, this study systematically revealed the microscopic mechanism and quantitative laws of capillary spontaneous imbibition in tight sandstone reservoirs, providing experimental evidence for the crude oil recovery mechanism during焖井 after fracturing, and directly guiding the optimization design of fracturing fluid return and焖井 systems.
Why it couldn’t be done before: The pore size in tight sandstone is extremely small (nanometer scale), and traditional mercury intrusion and core experiments cannot dynamically characterize fluid distribution and migration in pores in situ; the maturity of NMR core analysis technology and the widespread use of high-field instruments provide the basis for such research. Additionally, large-scale commercial shale oil/tight oil development in China (after 2015) created urgent engineering needs, driving funding and sample availability.
Impact: This paper was cited 108 times and became an important reference in the study of spontaneous imbibition in tight reservoirs, promoting the engineering direction of “midden well optimization—capillary drive” in China’s unconventional oil and gas field.
2. Stability analyses of dam abutments by 3D elasto-plastic finite-element method: A case study of Houhe gravity-arch dam in China (2005) Description: Using the Houhe gravity arch dam in China as a case study, a three-dimensional elasto-plastic finite element method was applied to systematically analyze the stability of the dam abutment, providing a numerical simulation framework applicable to actual engineering verification. This work was cited 39 times and represented the most influential achievement during this period.
Why it couldn’t be done before: Three-dimensional elasto-plastic finite element models require high computational resources, and three-dimensional rock mass simulations at engineering scale were not common in China before 2005; meanwhile, large-scale water conservancy projects in China (such as the Three Gorges Project) provided case sources and engineering background requirements.
Impact: It provided a methodological template for seismic stability analysis of gravity arch dams in China and has been continuously cited in geotechnical engineering literature.
3. Fluid flow with compaction and sand production in unconsolidated sandstone reservoir (2018) Description: Through single-phase displacement experiments, the coupled effects of compaction and sand production on flow patterns in unconsolidated sandstone reservoirs were quantitatively measured, and a fluid flow model considering reservoir damage was established, providing experimental evidence for predicting oil well productivity decline.
Why it couldn’t be done before: Specialized high-pressure core clamping devices to control compaction degree and sand production are difficult to implement; experimental operations on unconsolidated sandstone (sample preparation and encapsulation) are technically challenging, and relevant experimental data were scarce previously.
Impact: This paper was cited 23 times and provided an experimental basis for productivity assessment and sand control design in heavy oil and loose sandstone reservoirs (such as Liaohe oil field).

The variation mechanism of petrophysical properties and the effect of compaction on the relative permeability of an unconsolidated sandstone reservoir (2017) Description: A systematic study was conducted on the changes in petrophysical parameters (porosity, permeability) in unconsolidated sandstone reservoirs with compaction, especially quantifying the impact of compaction on the gas-water relative permeability curve, and revealing the mechanism of flow capacity decline during production.
Why it couldn’t be done before: Relative permeability experiments are usually carried out on consolidated cores; dynamic compaction + two-phase flow experiments on unconsolidated sandstone pose significant technical and equipment challenges, and such data have been lacking for a long time.
Impact: This paper was cited 18 times and filled the gap in compaction–flow coupling research on unconsolidated sandstone, offering practical reference for development scheme design of offshore heavy oil and loose sandstone reservoirs.

A SCREENING CANDIDATE RESERVOIR FOR GAS INJECTION WAY BASED ON CHARACTERISTIC PARAMETER’S COMPREHENSIVE WEIGHT OPTIMIZATION METHOD (2004) Description: A reservoir screening method based on comprehensive weight optimization of characteristic parameters was proposed for gas injection candidates, providing a quantitative decision-making framework for reservoir selection in CO₂/N₂/natural gas mixed phase drive, representing a systematic methodological contribution to early EOR engineering practices.
Why it couldn’t be done before: Early reservoir screening relied mostly on single-parameter empirical judgment, lacking a multi-parameter comprehensive quantitative evaluation method; meanwhile, large-scale CO₂-EOR experiments in China (early 2000s) provided data accumulation for refining screening criteria.
Impact: This paper was cited 6 times and provided reusable systematic screening ideas for pre-assessment of gas injection EOR projects in Chinese oil fields.

The middle period (2005—2011) shifted toward numerical simulation (three-dimensional elasto-plastic finite element) and geophysical field tests (CPTu, seismic waves, borehole geophysics), reflecting a trend toward precision in geotechnical engineering. The later period (2017—2019) completed the transition from macro-engineering to micro-mechanism: centered on high-pressure core physical experiments (single-phase/two-phase displacement, compaction loading devices) combined with NMR pore-scale characterization, supplemented by numerical simulation and theoretical models, representing the mainstream paradigm of contemporary reservoir physics research.

This pattern indicates that researchers identified key research opportunities with precise laboratory characterization capabilities during the rise of unconventional reservoirs, contributing specific and quantifiable academic contributions to the technology field of shale oil/tight oil development in China. Rating: Starlet (73.7/100) Basic Metrics Metric Value Institution Unknown h-index 65 Total Citations 17,649 Recent 5 Years Citations 1,099 Total Papers 369 Papers in Top Conferences 23 Publication Period 2003 - 2023 Semantic Scholar 5442167 Research Trajectory Yiran Chen’s academic trajectory shows three clear transitions. The first phase (2003–2007) focused on power optimization in traditional computer architectures, represented by Deterministic Clock Gating (DCG), representing a solid accumulation in the classic VLSI design field. The second phase (2008–2015) was the core period when he became a landmark figure in emerging storage fields: as spin-transfer torque (STT-RAM), phase-change memory (PCM), and memristor technologies moved from the laboratory to an engineeringable stage, Chen, with his deep expertise in circuits and architecture, rapidly led multiple main lines such as NVM device modeling, reliability analysis, cache architecture integration, and neuromorphic computing. He published frequently in top conferences like HPCA, DAC, and ICCAD, laying the methodological foundation for this field. The third phase (2016–present) is a explosive transformation: his 2016 paper on Structured Sparsity Learning received 2,478 citations, marking his entry into deep learning compression from a hardware-aware perspective. Subsequently, he produced high-impact works in directions such as distributed training communication compression (TernGrad), ReRAM-based accelerators (PipeLayer/GraphR), and AI security (adversarial attacks, federated learning defense). The key reason why Chen can become a leading figure across hardware and AI fields is that he always takes “how to run AI efficiently on constrained hardware” as the main line, integrating device physics, circuit design, architecture, and algorithm optimization into a unified research framework. This rare full-stack perspective allows him to lead his peers by many years when hardware-algorithm co-design becomes the mainstream trend.
Breakthrough Works 1. A novel architecture of the 3D stacked MRAM L2 cache for CMPs (2009) Description: For the first time, it systematically designed a three-dimensional stacked MRAM as an L2 cache for multi-core processors, conducting full-link evaluations from circuit modeling, thermal effect analysis to performance/power trade-offs at the architecture level, proving the engineering feasibility of NVM replacing traditional SRAM caches.
Why it couldn’t be done before: Key conditions were not mature before 2009: first, there was no mature circuit-level compact model for the magnetic tunnel junction (MTJ) process of STT-RAM; second, 3D chip stacking (TSV) technology had just entered the academic prototype stage; third, previous NVM research mainly remained at the device physics level, lacking a system-level methodology to integrate it into existing microprocessor storage layers. Chen’s team possessed both magnetic device modeling and computer architecture capabilities, precisely filling this interdisciplinary gap.
Impact: 453 citations, establishing the research paradigm of “NVM as an on-chip cache alternative,” directly triggering a large number of follow-up works on STT-RAM/PCM/RRAM cache architectures in the following decade, and establishing the methodological framework for coordinated evaluation of device-circuit-architecture.
2. Memristor Crossbar-Based Neuromorphic Computing System: A Case Study (2014) Description: Based on a memristor crossbar array, it systematically implemented and analyzed neuromorphic computing systems, covering complete engineering issues such as analog matrix-vector multiplication, non-linear activation implementation, and device variation-tolerant training, marking a landmark work in the transition from concept to engineeringizable neuromorphic computing with memristors.
Why it couldn’t be done before: Memristors were not manufactured and verified by HP Lab until 2008. Over the following years, sufficient experimental data on device characteristics (switching ratio, variation distribution, durability) was available for modeling. More importantly, mapping the analog conductance of memristors to neural network weights required a combined background in circuit design and neural network training theory—teams with such cross-domain vision were rare before 2014.
Impact: 338 citations, becoming a foundational comprehensive case study in memristor neuromorphic computing, and serving as the starting point for many subsequent “computing-in-Memory” accelerators.
3. Learning Structured Sparsity in Deep Neural Networks (2016) Description: Proposed a structured sparsity learning (SSL) method, applying group Lasso regularization to filter, channel, and convolution kernel shapes and network layer depths during training, enabling DNNs to automatically learn structured sparse patterns that can be directly mapped to hardware acceleration without specialized sparse computing hardware, thus achieving practical acceleration.
Why it couldn’t be done before: Previous network compression (e.g., Han Song 2015’s unstructured pruning) produced random sparsity that could not be efficiently utilized by general-purpose hardware, requiring dedicated sparse computing engines. The missing key insight was that no one realized that the granularity of sparsity constraints could be raised from the weight level to the structure level (entire column/entire layer), and group regularization could naturally emerge during training. Chen’s team reversed the hardware-implementability requirement into algorithm design, making this hardware-aware ML methodology extremely advanced at the time.
Impact: 2,478 citations, the highest-cited work in his paper list, completely changing the research paradigm in DNN compression, directly promoting “structured pruning” as the mainstream technical approach for model deployment in industry, and inspiring many subsequent channel and layer pruning methods.
4. TernGrad: Ternary Gradients to Reduce Communication in Distributed Deep Learning (2017) Description: Proposed using ternary gradients (-1, 0, +1) instead of full-precision floating-point gradients for gradient synchronization during distributed training, with theoretical proof of convergence and experimental verification that it significantly reduces communication bandwidth requirements while almost preserving accuracy during multi-GPU/multi-machine training.
Why it couldn’t be done before: Large-scale distributed deep learning training was not widespread before 2017, and the communication bottleneck became prominent only with the rise of large models such as AlexNet/ResNet. Prior quantitative research focused on weight compression at the inference end; using gradient quantization for training communication compression required a deep understanding of SGD convergence dynamics, as well as recognizing that the gradient direction rather than exact values was the newer key insight—this insight gained sufficient motivation to drive research in 2017 with the surge in distributed training demands.
Impact: 1,053 citations, establishing the subfield of “gradient compression” for distributed learning communication optimization, directly promoting series works such as 1-bit SGD and SignSGD, and having a lasting impact on large-scale AI training infrastructure.
5. PipeLayer: A Pipelined ReRAM-Based Accelerator for Deep Learning (2017) Description: Proposed a pipelined deep learning inference accelerator based on ReRAM, mapping neural network layers to ReRAM crossbar arrays and designing cross-layer pipeline data flow, achieving computing-in-Memory and high throughput inference, significantly outperforming GPU solutions in energy efficiency and speed.
Why it couldn’t be done before: Three conditions were required simultaneously: (1) the ReRAM device model was sufficiently mature to support system-level simulation; (2) the computational mode of deep learning inference (primarily dense matrix multiplication) was fully analyzed, making its natural match with analog crossbar arrays obvious; (3) ADC/DAC design techniques and peripheral circuit capabilities were sufficient to support mixed-signal system design. Before 2017, there was insufficient experimental data on ReRAM chip prototypes, and the modeling of tolerance to accuracy loss in DNNs was not yet mature.
Impact: 750 citations, becoming a landmark work on ReRAM computing-in-Memory accelerator, establishing the design principle of “eliminating ReRAM write latency bottlenecks through pipelining,” and directly initiating a large number of subsequent CIM accelerator research (ReTransformer, Lattice, etc.).
Research Directions Architecture modeling and system integration of non-volatile memory architectures (STT-RAM/RRAM/PCM) Computing-in-Memory and neuromorphic accelerators based on memristors/ReRAM Deep neural network compression and hardware-aware efficient inference (structured pruning, low-rank decomposition, quantization) AI security and robustness (adversarial attack generation and defense, data poisoning, federated learning security) Distributed machine learning and federated learning (communication compression, client selection, heterogeneity processing) Neural architecture search (NAS) and AutoML Methodological Evolution Chen’s methodological evolution shows a clear spiral upward “from bottom to top, then from top to bottom.” Early on (2003–2010), it centered on SPICE simulation and VLSI analysis tools, with methodology rooted in circuit design, focusing on precise modeling at the device and circuit levels. The transition period from 2010–2015 extended the methodology to the architecture level—introducing statistical variation analysis, Monte Carlo probability modeling, and a cross-layer (device-circuit-architecture) coordinated evaluation framework. This “from physics to system” vertical integration ability became its core competitiveness. Starting in 2016, the methodology shifted to a paradigm change: while retaining hardware implementation feasibility constraints, it turned to algorithm optimization, with SSL and TernGrad reflecting a reverse thinking of “algorithm design driven by hardware constraints.” After 2019, the methodology further expanded into system security, using game theory (attack-defense confrontation) and privacy computing frameworks to analyze federated learning security. In recent years, it has extended to LLM inference optimization. The overall trajectory is: single-layer precise modeling → cross-layer coordinated optimization → hardware-algorithm joint design → system security analysis, with each expansion based on the deep accumulation of the previous stage.
Domain Impact Yiran Chen’s impact on the field is reflected in three dimensions: First, in emerging memory fields, his STT-RAM/RRAM series works (2008–2015) established the foundational methodology for NVM computer architecture research, turning “using NVM to replace/supplement SRAM” from a physical idea into an engineeringable research agenda. Second, in deep learning system fields, the SSL paper (2,478 citations) and TernGrad (1,053 citations) are two textbook-level works: the former defined the technical direction of structured pruning, and the latter established the subfield of gradient compression. Together, they have received over 3,500 citations, profoundly influencing the technical approaches for AI chip deployment and large-scale training infrastructure. Third, in AI security and trustworthy AI, his team made foundational contributions in directions such as adversarial samples, data poisoning attacks, and federated learning defense, promoting a systematic understanding of the vulnerabilities of AI systems in academia. His unique value is that, as one of the few scholars with high-citation works simultaneously in top computer architecture conferences (HPCA/MICRO/ISCA) and machine learning conferences (NeurIPS/ICML/CVPR/ICLR), he continuously acts as a “translator” and “bridge builder” between the hardware and AI communities. His h-index of 65 and nearly 18,000 total citations are at the top level in this composite field.

A new quantitative method to evaluate the spatial distribution of fibres in composites: the degree of randomness (2023) Description: A new quantitative index—‘degree of randomness’—was proposed to assess the randomness of fiber spatial distribution in composite materials, providing a measurable mathematical description for fiber distribution uniformity.
Why it couldn’t be done before: Previously, there was a lack of a unified quantitative framework for evaluating the randomness of fiber spatial distribution. Researchers relied on visual judgment or indirect indicators (such as nearest-neighbor distances), and there were no dimensionless indicators for cross-material system comparison. The key insight was transplanting the concept of randomness from statistical physics into micro-structure analysis of composite materials.
Impact: It provided a standardized evaluation scale for assessing subsequent virtual micro-structure generation algorithms, directly supporting the algorithm comparison work published in the same year, which was cited 6 times.

Comparison of three algorithms generating virtual microstructures in terms of the degree of randomness (2023) Description: Based on the ‘degree of randomness’ index, the performance of three algorithms for generating virtual microstructures of composite materials was systematically compared to evaluate each algorithm’s ability to reproduce real fiber random distribution.
Why it couldn’t be done before: Previously, there was a lack of unified evaluation criteria for comparing different virtual micro-structure generation algorithms, and each algorithm study was independent and unable to be compared horizontally. The introduction of the ‘degree of randomness’ method made such systematic comparison possible.
Impact: Cited 16 times, this is currently the most influential work of the researcher, providing an algorithm selection reference for the digital twin and multi-scale modeling communities in composite materials.

Visual encoder single-modal ARI dropped to approximately 0.0 because hires coordinates were misused for full-resolution images, causing all patches to enter the background region and destroying embedding variance. Solution: Implement an automatic scaling function in VisionExtractor to adjust via 1/scale_factor; bypass NaN barcode matching loops; clean up corrupted caches. In all slices, ARI recovery is very fast.
Key Insight: The coordinate space mismatch between downsampled metadata and original high-resolution images causes samples to be pushed into the background region, inadvertently destroying embedding variance.
2. scGPT TransformerModel couldn’t load checkpoints due to the lack of fast_transformer instance attributes, forcing silent fallback to default settings, resulting in random changes in 17.7% of attention weights. Key Insight: Strict checkpoint loading hides key attribute deficiencies by silently falling back to defaults; explicit state persistence is required, rather than relying on flexible initialization parameters.

Solution: Forced execution using CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES="" and JAX_PLATFORMS=cpu bypass flags; mapped PID via nvidia-smi to target termination of idle inference servers.
Key Insight: Machine learning frameworks usually initialize the device backend immediately upon import, while long-running VLA servers silently retain VRAM during initialization; strict environment isolation and periodic cluster audits are necessary.
4. BC-RNN Coffee task achieved a success rate of only 0% despite standard training completion, because the configuration template only maps low-dimensional keys, completely ignoring the required 57-dimensional object state. Solution: Fix the YAML generation script to inject task-specific ‘object’ overrides, verify modality existence via HDF5 Schema, and regenerate the configuration; restore training convergence.
Key Insight: Precise multi-stage operation tasks require explicit spatial/motion object state inputs; relying solely on RGB images fails when fine alignment is needed rather than simple geometric stacking.
5. robosuite/robomimic observation vector mismatch (CHW/84x84 vs HWC/256x256) and tyro CLI parameter assumptions caused batch processing bottlenecks and silent runtime failures. Solution: Add automatic checkpoints to detect modalities, implement HWC to CHW conversion in the strategy adapter, correct force/overwrite boolean flag to –no-overwrite syntax, and verify based on actual CLI help output.
Key Insight: Cross-framework integration requires strict metadata alignment; modern parameter parsers enforce symmetric boolean flags and require precise signature verification, rather than assuming standard positions.
General Issues 6. AI-generated daily JSON reports contain markdown code wrapping or truncation, causing local json.loads() parsing crashes during cross-device aggregation. Solution: Implement a robust extraction layer with markdown stripping and dynamic range detection, upgrade API calls to enforce strict response_format mode, and isolate routing via asynchronous timeout handlers.

Configured Xcode build phases to automatically increment CFBundleVersion while bypassing the sandbox restrictions. Issues and Solutions Key Issues 1. Due to failed Flash Attention key mappings, catastrophic silent weight corruption occurred during scGPT checkpoint loading, while Visium HD spatial image micro-pixels appeared; Xcode build scripts failed due to sandbox restrictions. Solution: Add missing use_fast_transformer initialization to trigger correct PyTorch key mappings; dynamically adjust visualization parameters based on sensor point diameter; disable the user script sandbox mechanism to allow modification via PlistBuddy after compilation.
Key Insight: Silent weight skipping in deep learning and hardware-specific scaling factors in spatial visualization may cause downstream metrics to fail completely, requiring active verification; macOS build sandbox requires explicit configuration overrides for dynamic file operations.
2. Enterprise proxy variables hijack TCP/WebSocket traffic on HPC nodes, causing WebSocket client connections to be rejected despite open ports; version mismatches in robosuite/robomimic cause simulation environment crashes. Solution: Explicitly disable http_proxy and https_proxy settings during HPC job initialization to enable direct point-to-point routing; adjust PYTHONPATH to use a unified dependency directory to override local conda packages, and implement missing geometric bounding box methods for composite objects.
Key Insight: HPC environments often inherit restrictive HTTP proxies that interfere with alternative port communication without warning; the simulation framework is highly sensitive to package version drift, requiring a unified dependency root and explicit environment registration hooks.
General Issues 3. macOS application session management has conflicts in window notifications, old bookmarks status, and unimplemented power-saving stub issues, reducing multi-monitor user experience during rapid wake/sleep cycles.Solution: Deploy a proxy tool to track SharedWallpaperWindowManager bindings, identify duplicate NSWindow observers, fix UserDefaults clear keys, and develop an implementation plan for stable screen state synchronization. Key Insight: Multi-screen macOS applications require strict window lifecycle management ownership tracking; old states persist when the UserDefaults clear key is missing or observer callbacks trigger asynchronously during rapid session transitions.
4. SLURM partition permission errors related to QOS/account mismatches, combined with GPU memory saturation caused by zombie checkpoint loading processes, hinders new allocations. Solution: Adjust job submission methods to use correct account mappings and --gres=gpu:1 to bypass CPU/memory quotas; inject tasks into active steps using srun --overlap, and hijack existing high VRAM zombie PIDs instead of creating duplicate servers.
Key Insight: Enterprise HPC clusters strictly associate partition access with account/QOS hierarchies rather than node availability; zombie processes in shared GPU allocation severely fragment memory, requiring pre-checking partition allocation and process reuse policies via nvidia-smi.

Over-reliance on truncated single job logs to verify training status, causing initial misunderstandings about checkpoint completion status until the parent directory cross-reference corrected the inference results. Learning Outcomes Key Learning Outcomes Dependence on silent weight skipping or threshold-based parameter loading requires immediate verification of downstream metrics, as minor initialization omissions in deep learning definitions may lead to catastrophic unobservable data loss. Multimodal fusion and specialized architectures (such as PCA-UNI2-STAIG) performed significantly better than simple series or single-modal baselines in spatial coherence benchmarks using unlabeled high-resolution tissue data. Custom robot simulation environments and evaluation clients require explicit environment registration hooks and a unified dependency root; enterprise proxy variables must be explicitly disabled before initializing original socket connections on restricted HPC nodes. Tasks Architecture and Strategy ✅ HDD_POOL Storage Audit — Analyzed the directory sizes under user accounts in the XYFS01 shared system to identify major consumers and estimate total usage. ✅ Slurm GPU Node Configuration — Explored available partitions, command options, and secure connection methods to prepare for AI training workloads. ✅ M14 Baseline Evaluation Review — Investigated the current evaluation scripts and results of Pi0/BC-RNN policies in error recovery scenarios. Issues and Solutions Key Issues 1. Direct SSH access to Slurm GPU nodes is blocked by cluster security policies. Solution: Switch to salloc/tmux and sbatch workflows, and validate through documentation checks.
Key Insight: The cluster relies on pam_slurm_adopt to enforce task-bound access; session persistence requires terminal multiplexing or batch submission, rather than direct network connection.
General Issues 2. Scanning large directories causes severe timeouts during storage audits. Solution: Use du commands with explicit timeout and depth limits for parallel background processing to safely collect partial results.
Key Insight: Metadata operations on the Lustre file system require high I/O; large-scale audits need secure rollback strategies and partition scanning.
Human and AI Approaches Strategic Level Evaluation Dataset Configuration Scope Role Method Human Users recall previous instructions, switch evaluation to training set, and expect immediate execution based on implicit context. AI AI searches the file system history, finds no such changes, analyzes existing configurations, and asks about specific technical definitions of seed reset and data splitting. Analysis of Differences: Humans operate from advanced project planning memory; AI strictly follows stateless validation protocols, highlighting the gap between expected pipeline changes and actual code library implementation status.
AI Limitations General Limitations Due to file system I/O timeouts, accurate estimation of large directory sizes is impossible; iterative rollback strategies are required instead of automatic completion. Lack of persistent memory for vague past instructions, resulting in inability to provide clear file references when asking about code modifications. Lessons Learned Key Experiences The success rate of baseline policies under error injection scenarios is nearly zero, indicating severe distributed migration, and validates the architectural adjustment toward human participation in fine-tuning (M15). Cluster security policies like pam_slurm_adopt strictly limit compute node access; stable tasks require multiplexing or batch scripts, not direct network connections. Daily Report — 2026-02-23 General Overview Completed Tasks: Identified and resolved major serialization bottlenecks in the visual encoder fusion process, removed restrictive hard-coded constraints to support flexible multi-model benchmarks, stabilized large-scale robot policy data collection and long-term training processes, and avoided silent crashes and environment mismatches. Implementation Methods: Implemented sparse matrix vectorization, dynamic scaling adapters, and batch Transformer inference to improve performance; optimized the data collector’s fault-tolerant log skipping; updated Slurm launch scripts with non-buffered I/O, clear recovery checkpoints, and error capture mechanisms; automated statistical benchmark data reporting using defensive scipy alternatives. Impact: Initialization/training speed of complex fusion models increased by more than 20 times, enabling unrestricted cross-encoder evaluation across 11 spatial transcriptomics sections, maintaining continuous evaluation processes under 649 parallel scenarios, and allowing continuous monitoring and precise synchronization of metrics during multi-hour policy training. DCC Completed Tasks: Performed pipeline orchestration, iterative refactoring, background benchmark execution, and comparative visualization generation for the MIHD framework. Implementation Methods: Utilized AI-assisted code editing, Python syntax validation, dynamic cache management, and Bash task monitoring; integrated experimental outputs into structured CSV format and spatial plots. Impact: Achieved direct running optimization without external dependencies, maintained conda environment consistency during refactoring cycles, and provided actionable clustering insights for downstream preprocessing strategies. tianhe Completed Tasks: Coordinated parallel SLURM workloads for M14/M16 baseline analysis, VLA evaluation recovery, and Pi0.5 Phoenix LoRA training recovery. Implementation Methods: Applied targeted patches to collector.py to achieve graceful error handling; updated the training shell script with state persistence and non-buffered output flags; automated version tracking and milestone synchronization via file modifications. Impact: Eliminated pipeline interruptions caused by mixed scenario fingerprint mismatches, ensured continuous training without silent exits, and maintained cross-project version consistency without manual intervention. Key CPU and architecture optimizations were applied to the multi-omics fusion workflow, resolving environment fingerprint conflicts that caused large-scale robot evaluation interruptions, and stabilized long-term policy training through resilient monitoring and checkpoint strategies.
Tasks Architecture and Strategy 🔄 Long-term Policy Training Stability and Recovery Logic — Restored Pi0.5 Phoenix LoRA training via clear checkpoint recovery, non-buffered stdout wrapping, and SLURM error capture mechanisms; corrected evaluation environment initialization and quaternion processing to ensure reproducible state tracking. ✅ Fusion Pipeline CPU Optimization and Architecture Decoupling — Resolved O(n²) edge weight loops, sequential spot-level Transformer calls, and old cache interference; removed hard-coded UNI encoder restrictions, allowing dynamic selection of visual variant paths in the MIHD framework. ✅ Large-scale Evaluation Recovery and Fingerprint Conflict Resolution — Diagnosed EnvironmentMismatchError crashes during natural/pulse scenario collection, implemented defensive log skipping in the data collector, and successfully restored parallel Pi0/Pi0.5 evaluations for 649 scenarios. ✅ Cross-encoder Benchmark Testing and Optimization Trade-off Analysis — Performed large-scale staig_fusion tests on all 11 DLPFC regions, compared baseline and scan_cluster optimization metrics, and recorded performance differences—while dimensionality reduction benefits apply to simple fusion, they negatively impact high-capacity learners. ✅ Statistical Benchmark Report and Pipeline Restart — Executed m14_cpu baseline analysis including Fleiss’ kappa reliability test and Kruskal-Wallis discriminant test, added defensive handling for degraded scipy inputs, and updated project documentation to v4.12 version. Issues and Solutions Key Issues 1. Serialization bottlenecks in fusion loops (nested Python loops for edge weights, sequential forward processing) and hard-coded architecture restrictions caused severe CPU/GPU idleness and limited multi-encoder flexibility. Solution: Replaced iterative calculations with NumPy/scipy vectorization, filled variable-length neighbor tensors for native GPU parallelism, solved ViT patch incompatibility through dynamic scaling, and decoupled routing from strict encoder dependencies.
Key Insight: Graph-based preprocessing and sample-level Transformer inference are essentially serialized; unified tensor filling enables full batch parallelism. Traditional architectures often limit modern multi-model pipelines unless explicitly decoupled at the routing layer.
2. The mixed dataset collection pipeline crashed fatally due to inconsistent XML hashes between generated and natural scenarios, while long-term training scripts silent exited due to Python output buffering and missing checkpoint logic. Solution: Inserted EnvironmentMismatchError fallback mechanisms in the collector to log warnings and gracefully skip incompatible initialization; updated launch scripts with PYTHONUNBUFFERED flag, clear recovery flags, error capture mechanisms, and reliable evaluation environment initialization.
Key Insight: Mixed data pipelines require conditional fault tolerance rather than strict mismatch interruption protocols. Multi-hour GPU workloads need defensive I/O configuration, persistent state tracking, and reproducible environment initialization to handle preemption or silent failures.
General Issues 3. Statistical analysis failed on degraded group inputs (zero variance/single group cases), default initial spatial visualization output was a single panel rather than a comparison layout, requiring manual correction. Solution: Wrapped scipy statistical calls with defensive variance checks, returning valid default dictionaries; corrected plotting prompts to enforce multi-panel comparison structures, and automatically cached results.
Key Insight: Automated scientific pipelines must anticipate edge-case inputs and provide fallback distributions, with explicit enforcement of output format constraints during program generation.
Human and AI Approaches Strategic Level Strategic task decomposition, runtime orchestration, and pipeline automation | Roles | Methods | |——|——| | Human | Defined structured priority queues for multiple milestone dependencies (M13/M14/M16), manually verified scenario counts, mapped bottlenecks to optimizers, and inferred trade-offs in visual optimization metric representation. | | AI | Performed automatic dependency verification, dynamic file path checks, parallel CLI task allocation, applied defensive code patches for mismatched environments and statistical edge cases, and maintained real-time documentation synchronization without manual intervention. |
Analysis of Differences: Humans are responsible for high-level experimental design, strategic priority mapping, and domain-intuitive architecture trade-offs; AI operates at runtime orchestration level, automatically diagnoses hidden failure modes, applies resilient script patterns, and maintains system state via automated tool calls. Insights on dimensionality compression effects are calculated and verified through AI-driven metric aggregation.
AI Limitations General Limitations Default initial visualization settings produce a single-panel layout instead of a comparison structure, early task planning processes intermittently interrupt due to system ExitPlanMode constraints, requiring manual re-engagement. Obsolete compilation cache artifacts and TaskOutput API timeouts hinder real-time progress visibility, necessitating manual file system cleanup and backup filesystem checks during real-time refactoring and long-background polling. Lessons Learned Key Experiences Visual embedding optimization improved clustering performance in simple fusion, but caused performance degradation in high-capacity learners due to information loss; downstream model compatibility must be dynamically verified to prevent hidden bypasses or shape mismatches. Large-scale physical simulation and multi-hour GPU training processes require defensive fault tolerance: gracefully skip logs for different environment fingerprints, combined with clear checkpoint persistence and non-buffered standard output, to ensure observability during latent failures. Framework correctness and policy behavior quality require different verification layers: integration tests confirm code paths, while GPU deployment combined with video visualization is essential for diagnosing underfitting. Architecture Pure visual encoders inevitably reach a plateau in fine spatial stratification without self-supervised constraints or multimodal fusion; task-feature mismatch is an architectural feature rather than a implementation flaw. Solution: Users corrected the architecture direction: integrating CacheManager directly into the existing benchmark script and adding variant tracking, instead of creating parallel tools that might introduce preprocessing drift.
Key Insight: Utilizing existing process infrastructure is more robust and maintainable than building isolated evaluation wrappers, especially when strict feature normalization consistency is required.
2. The low STAIG fusion ARI score produced by eval_scan_fusion.py is due to the lack of alignment configuration, resulting in dual normalization by external preprocessing and internal StandardScaler. Solution: Identified the root cause and recorded that passing the correct staig_alignment_config to apply_fusion() triggers align_staig=True, automatically skipping redundant scaling in the trainer.
Key Insight: When evaluating models using built-in feature alignment or normalization layers, the external preprocessing process must pass a clear override flag or completely skip normalization to avoid signal distortion.
3. BC-RNN policy evaluation crashes during expansion due to mismatched input dimensions (checkpoint expects 65-dimensional, environment provides 37-dimensional) and state_info incorrectly replacing raw observations. Solution: Fixed the key mapping in _to_robosuite_obs() to match the training mode, and updated generate_from_single_rollout and capture_single_rollout methods to pass the raw robosuite dictionary during initialization.
Key Insight: The policy inference process must strictly maintain the original observation pattern during expansion, as internal state extractors often lose or compress keys required by pre-trained adapters.
General Issues 4. Failure of MimicGen data set generation in RoboMimic 0.3.0 is due to passing outdated kwargs to create_env_for_data_processing, causing environment instantiation crashes. Solution: Dynamically checked the real-time API signature, updated the wrapper to pass only supported parameters conditionally, and automatically fallback when expected fields are missing from environment metadata.
Key Insight: Version locking of third-party ML environments is crucial; dynamic signature checks or strict version restrictions can prevent hidden API damage during data flow execution.

Daily Report — 2026-02-19 Overview of Daily Work Completed work: Integrated core MIHD spatial transcriptomics research, and simultaneously developed the second-phase validation process for error recovery benchmarks. Specific tasks include comprehensive metric documentation, a literature review on pathological base models, implementation and benchmarking of self-supervised clustering enhancement techniques (STEGO, BYOL+GAT, SCAN), construction of large-scale datasets (M12), verification of error classification statistics (M13), and planning of baseline evaluation (M14). Cross-domain work also includes extensive project documentation refactoring, stabilization of automated processes, and remote environment fixes. Implementation methods: Implemented a self-supervised head module using custom PyTorch modules, ran GPU tasks for data augmentation in parallel, wrote statistical verification scripts (Cohen’s kappa, Kruskal-Wallis), and integrated large project documents using automated refactoring techniques. Algorithm stability was ensured through L2 normalization and float64 precision buffering, while infrastructure resilience was maintained by targeted SSH configuration fixes and cache bypass mechanisms across compute nodes. Impact: These efforts established a robust technical foundation for evaluating visual encoders and gene expression benchmarks, verified the advantages of combining self-supervised feature extractors with transcriptome data, and achieved crash-resistant, distributed evaluation processes. The integrated documents and repaired remote access significantly reduced cross-team friction, accelerated iterative research cycles, and brought the development process into line with academic publishing standards. Implementation methods: Utilized interactive terminal sessions, automated code library extraction tools, and iterative Python scripts to analyze rm_ideal.py, visual embedding processes, and configuration schemes. Applied structured patching for CLI parameter parsing, contrast learning modules, and evaluation scheduling logic, while managing GPU task orchestration. Impact: The centralized high-level architecture design and initial module writing in DCC enabled the self-supervised framework to quickly prototype, directly supporting subsequent benchmark validation, and established clear baselines for multimodal fusion experiments. Implementation methods: Diagnosed that the issue stemmed from incompatibility between Windows OpenSSH and Unix-based connection reuse commands. Cleaned up expired socket files, disabled conflicting parameters in .ssh/config, verified access permissions via CLI fallback, and clarified job scheduling policies for restricted nodes. Impact: By restoring reliable gateway connections to cluster resources, critical local development obstacles were eliminated, environmental degradation was prevented, and subsequent distributed evaluation processes were not blocked. tianhe Completed work: Served as the main workstation for expanding the M12 dataset for error recovery benchmarks, deploying M13 classification verification scripts, large-scale parallel simulations, and comprehensive project documentation refactoring. Started developing the second-phase roadmap. Implementation methods: Used Claude Code to generate multi-agent tasks, automatically generated unit tests, started Mujoco simulations in parallel, and collected statistics from split repositories. Applied versioning constraints to document updates, adjusted environment variables (CUDA/EGL) to ensure stable GPU execution. Impact: Accelerating theoretical planning into validated code libraries reduced document redundancy by 50% without breaking structural hierarchy, and established recoverable processes that allow continued operation—critical for submitting papers in the second phase. Today, basic MIHD research and advanced error recovery benchmark infrastructure were combined, focusing on comprehensive metric documentation, self-supervised visual encoder clustering enhancement techniques, expansion of large-scale datasets, classification verification, and strict cross-platform environment optimization.
Tasks Architecture and Strategy ✅ Documentation of MIHD metrics and standardization of visual encoder processes — Comprehensive bilingual documents were generated regarding RM-IDEAL scoring calculation and visual encoder architecture. Extensive literature research was conducted on UNI2, spEMO, STAIG, SPADE, and HEST-1k, while the benchmark visualization process was modified, high-resolution H&E reference panels were integrated, and batch output charts were regenerated using cache embedding. ✅ Implementation of self-supervised clustering engine and multimodal fusion benchmarks — Custom PyTorch modules for STEGO spatial contrast loss, BYOL+GAT feature optimization, and SCAN clustering consistency head modules were built. InfoNCE discrepancy issues were resolved through L2 normalization and precision constraints, spatial coordinate loading mismatches were fixed, and GPU benchmark tests were run in parallel, demonstrating that SCAN combined with PCA gene features significantly improves ARI/NMI metrics. ✅ Implementation of error recovery benchmarks M12/M13 and planning for second-phase validation — Data set size was expanded to 454 scenarios using MimicGen enhancement techniques and hierarchical segmentation. Reliability scripts for Cohen’s/Fleiss’ kappa, Kruskal-Wallis discriminant analysis, and cross-strategy JSONL merging were implemented. Recovery logic was added to the episode collector, and fault-tolerant distributed execution was achieved through offset/limited slicing. Implementation and Fixes ✅ Refactoring of project architecture documentation and optimization of CLAUDE.md — A large project document of ~1500 lines was reduced to 763 lines, redundant chapters were removed, tutorial content was migrated, code library statistics were updated, and all target hierarchical structures were preserved. Type counts were corrected, conftest.py fixed-point references were added, and the document structure aligned with long-term research trajectories. ✅ Fixes to remote SSH configuration and stabilization of cross-device environments — The conflict between Windows OpenSSH and Unix-based connection reuse on high-performance compute nodes was diagnosed and resolved. CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES and MUJOCO_EGL_DEVICE_ID variables were adjusted to prevent simulator crashes, pytest numpy boolean comparison failures were fixed, and explicit cache bypass flags were enforced to accurately track metrics. Problems and Solutions Key Problems 1. Pre-trained pathological base models exhibit severe distribution shifts in fine cortical layer recognition and clustering anatomy due to surgical-oriented pre-training and subtle morphological gradients, causing these regions to be artificially distorted. Solution: Abandoned the original frozen encoder clustering and adopted target-domain self-supervised adaptation strategies (such as STEGO feature matching蒸馏, BYOL potential guidance), combined with on-the-fly optimization. Key insight: The base model optimized for coarse organizational phenotypes lacks the micro-scale spatial gradient retention required for fine domain transformation; unsupervised clustering alone cannot verify cross-modal alignment and requires specific domain-target adjustments.
2. InfoNCE loss converges to NaN, and downstream fusion methods crash due to dense similarity matrix overflow, float32 precision limitations, and shape mismatches in old coordinate loaders. Solution: Applied sklearn L2 normalization pre-projection, limited similarity to float64 tensors, repaired the data loader to extract coordinates directly from adata.obsm, and replaced inline shell commands with independent execution scripts with cache bypass flags.
Key insight: Contrast targets with wide spatial neighborhoods require strict numerical stability protocols; redundant coordinate acquisition introduces dimensional mismatch and disrupts the unified evaluation scheduling mechanism.
3. Distributed benchmark tests lasting 15 hours are highly susceptible to node timeout, crashes, and environmental failures, lacking an automatic recovery mechanism or consistent OS-specific configurations. Solution: Integrated episode-based recovery mechanisms in the collector, skipped completed tuples; implemented offset/limited CLI slicing for fault-tolerant sub-batch processing; disabled Windows OpenSSH ControlMaster multiplexing to clear outdated sockets; aligned GPU device environment variables.
Key insight: HPC workflows require explicit state recovery mechanisms rather than external checkpoints; cross-platform development networks need strict parameter auditing to prevent implicit hardware degradation or persistent connection failures.
General Problems 4. Iterative document updates lead to information accumulation and redundant architectural descriptions, causing large markdown files to exceed the context window during roadmap planning. Solution: Applied block-based automated refactoring, retained all operational milestone hierarchies, used pattern matching for targeted structural editing, and verified completeness via Grep before final submission.
Key insight: Appendive document updates inevitably separate from infrastructure realities; strategic compression must balance information density with organizational tracking needs to maintain long-term agent introduction efficiency.
Human and AI Approaches Experimental Rigor & Isolating and Automated Scalability of Benchmarks Role Method Human Strictly isolated pure single-modal morphology benchmarks to prevent false effectiveness inflation caused by multimodal ablation, prioritizing high-precision single-task analysis, and forcing manual remote operations to recover data despite higher costs. AI Designed highly parallelized pipelines to cover multi-task expansion, automatic/Oracle data generation, and fast scanning protocols; initially included image embedding as an independent method in multimodal datasets to maximize output speed. Difference analysis: Human reasoning emphasizes scientific validity and limits scope to ensure reliable conclusions; AI optimizes broad automation, but quickly adjusts when clear mathematical isolation standards are established.
Strategic Verification Architecture vs. Tactical Execution and Diagnosis Role Method Human Provided structured theoretical frameworks (FMEA mapping, statistical thresholds), specified exact chapter/model source tracking, and corrected diagnostic directions when visual artifacts were misattributed to transcriptome crashes. AI Generated plans via sub-task generation, wrote complete PyTorch modules, identified numerically unstable tensor operations, refactored coordinate loading logic, and synthesized quantitative benchmarks. Difference analysis: Humans manage high-level experimental design, threshold-driven transitions, and verification standards; AI designs low-level implementations, iterates debugging of training dynamics, and calculates metrics, requiring explicit corrections to shift analysis focus from architecture to benchmark effectiveness.
Document Constraint Management & Terminological Consistency Role Method Human Rejected pure syntax compression proposals that might threaten nested milestone tracking; directly intervened when AI research plans rely on ambiguous terms related to recovery training data and standard demonstrations. AI Prioritized reducing information density and eliminating cross-references, generated data acquisition strategies that are contextually inconsistent but structurally coherent until constrained by precise domain definitions. Difference analysis: Humans balance technical documentation standards with organizational workflow needs; AI focuses on structural optimization until it is guided to retain functional hierarchy levels and reduce markers.
AI Limitations It is difficult to directly access the full academic paywall, and it is hard to distinguish independent single-modal benchmarks from multimodal ablation studies, requiring repeated fallback queries and strict user constraint filtering to separate pure morphological performance metrics. The limited autonomous environment perception leads to initial CPU usage despite GPU requirements, and visual artifacts are misattributed to incorrect model sources until precise Slurm strategy context is obtained through operational feedback. Context window limitations force manual segmentation of large repository documents during roadmap updates, and automatic code generation occasionally produces Shell escape conflicts or numpy boolean patterns that violate existing project norms. Lessons Learned Key Lessons Learned Pure visual spatial clustering yields low ARI (~0.1–0.2); morphological features alone cannot capture cortical details, so multimodal fusion or target-specific self-supervised alignment is mathematically necessary for effective domain transformation. Dense contrast targets and long-term distributed evaluation require strict input L2 normalization, float64 precision buffering, explicit cache bypass flags, and episode-based recovery logic to prevent gradient explosion, stale reads, and state loss. Practical Lessons — In abstract planning, human participation in coordinating loop terminology is crucial; clear constraints on experimental scope and validation standards avoid structurally reasonable but practically mismatched workflows, while block document refactoring must preserve organizational hierarchy while pursuing syntactic simplicity. Parallel benchmark tests on spatial transcriptomics data show that compared to frozen encoders, SCAN processed features have a significant advantage over PCA gene embedding, and the visualization process has been updated to include high-resolution H&E reference panels for direct morphological correlation analysis.

A recoverable data collector was implemented, and distributed M12 dataset expansion was achieved through offset/limit slicing techniques. 2. ccusage returns cost=0 for Claude-opus-4-6, causing severe token cost tracking failure (actual $43 on February 17 shows $0.90, which is 13 times underestimated) Solution: A backup pricing mechanism was implemented in the fetch_ccusage() function of daily_summary.py through post-processing logic _fix_zero_cost_models(). A dictionary _FALLBACK_PRICING was added (opus-4-6: input $5/model, output $25/model, caching creation $6.25/model, caching reading $0.50/model) to calculate correct costs. Field name errors were fixed (mb.get(‘model’) → mb.get(‘modelName’) or mb.get(‘model’)) to ensure compatibility. Logs for February 13–17 were re-exported, and the displayed costs were corrected from $3–7 per day to actual $18–48 per day.
Key Findings: Defects in third-party tool pricing cannot be directly fixed—a local backup mechanism is used as a practical solution. LiteLLM uses versioned model names (anthropic.claude-opus-4-6-v1 with -v1 suffix), while Claude Code logs use simplified names (claude-opus-4-6), leading to systematic mismatches. The backup design must trigger only when anomalies occur (cost=0) to maintain backward compatibility when upstream fixes appear. Cost tracking errors can lead to over 90% underestimation (13 times in this case), severely affecting resource planning decisions. Always verify the output format of third-party tools by printing the original data rather than inferring from documents.
3. The Tianhe non-pulse injector (friction/pose perturbation/gripping bias) crashes when trying to parse body/geometry IDs in the MuJoCo model due to “AttributeError: no attribute mj_name2id” Solution: The model.body_name2id() and model.geom_name2id() methods are wrapped by robosuite instead of direct mujoco.mj_name2id(). An auxiliary function _resolve_body_id() is added, first trying “name” then trying “name_main” suffix (robosuite naming convention). The try/except mechanism is used to handle missing bodies gracefully.
Key Findings: Robosuite wraps MuJoCo through its own API layer and adds a _main suffix after the object name. Direct calls to MuJoCo C API bypass the framework layer and cause crashes—only the wrapping function provided by the framework must be used for name conversion. The robot simulation framework layer abstracts the original physics engine; direct API calls bypassing the framework cause crashes. Before modification, always check valid reference code in the same codebase (e.g., ImpulseInjector) for the same code library.
4. The Tianhe BC-RNN strategy crashes due to KeyError 'object' because the obs dictionary generated by StateExtractor contains the key ‘object-state’, while robomimic training data uses the key ‘object’ (different robosuite tasks have inconsistent key names: PickPlace uses object-state, Lift uses object) Solution: A key mapping was added in _to_robosuite_obs() Strategy 1, converting the object-state alias into object before returning the original obs. The backup solution for Strategy 3 was updated, merging objects from StateExtractor into a object key using pos + quat. Verified by 79 unit tests and GPU integration tests—KeyError has been eliminated.
Key Findings: Robosuite automatically adds a -state suffix after grouping modalities (e.g., object → object-state), but training data uses the original names. The adapter layer must fill this naming convention gap. Different robosuite tasks have inconsistent observation key naming rules. Manual reconstruction of obs cannot guarantee consistency with key names during training. The safest approach is to directly pass the original env.step() return value via a key alias. This indicates that cross-task compatibility requires either (a) a unified obs format or (b) a clear key mapping layer.
5. LLMs often return corrupted JSON in structured reports: unescaped quotes, incomplete objects, extra text, or truncation near token limits, leading to parsing failures and workflow interruptionsSolution: A four-stage backup parser was implemented: (1) directly use json.loads(), (2) extract json blocks, (3) find a complete JSON object based on deep matching of bracket structures, (4) call the LLM to fix the corrupted JSON. For APIs that support this feature, use tool_use (Anthropic) or response_format=json_object (OpenAI) to force valid JSON. Key Insight: Structured data generated by LLMs require multiple backup strategies for defensive parsing. The native JSON mode (tool_use/json_object) can significantly reduce errors, but cannot completely avoid failures. Using the LLM fix as the final backup solution can build a robust process. Each backup layer handles a specific type of failure: code blocks handle Markdown formatting, bracket matching handles truncation issues, and the fix handles syntax errors.
6. The BC-RNN model has a 0% success rate after resolving KeyError—the robot hovers over the box but cannot approach the target Solution: Three visual videos (400 frames each) were generated to show the robot’s behavior. The root cause was identified as a training insufficient checkpoint (epoch 600, limited demo data), not a framework bug. The video shows the robot hovers but never tries to grab. More training epochs or better checkpoints are needed.
Key Insight: Even if unit tests pass, GPU integration tests are crucial. BC-RNN passed all 79 unit tests, but actual operation on GPU reveals 0% SR issues. Video visualization is important for diagnosing behavioral quality issues in robots. Framework correctness and model quality require different verification strategies: unit tests/integration tests confirm code logic; video visualization reveals behavior quality.
7. SSH connections to the Tianhe HPC cluster often disconnect, causing Claude Code sessions to be lost and work to fail; VS Code Remote SSH is also affected Solution: A multi-layer deep defense scheme was implemented: (1) set up SSH keep-alive on both ends (15-second heartbeat, 90-second tolerance), (2) use tmux sessions for persistence so processes continue after disconnection, (3) write Claude-tmux scripts to restore sessions with one-click via automatic proxy, (4) comment out the automatic proxy in .bashrc to isolate the user environment from shared accounts, (5) write local client configuration instructions for ControlMaster multiplexing and automatic SSH reconnection scripts.
Key Insight: Network instability requires multiple layers of redundancy: protocol layer (TCP keep-alive), SSH layer (ControlMaster), application layer (tmux + automatic reconnection). No single layer is sufficient to ensure production environment reliability. tmux separates session state from connection status, achieving true recovery capability. Session-level proxy configuration (not global .bashrc) avoids affecting other shared account users. When working on shared server accounts, each environment modification (PATH, proxy, alias) must consider multi-user impacts.
8. The multi-device daily report workflow requires a synchronization mechanism—device-independent exports but merged reports require access to all device exports, and merged devices may not have access to these files Solution: A two-layer rclone synchronization is used: export files are uploaded to <remote>/logs/, merged reports are uploaded to <remote>/reports/. The merge --sync flag is added before LLM aggregation to download logs/files from all devices. A _merged_devices tracking mechanism is implemented to avoid re-summarizing already processed devices.
Key Insight: Distributed workflows require clear synchronization points. Separating original export files (logs/) from aggregated output (reports/) prevents circular dependencies. Idempotent design (skipping processed content) can be safely run again without expensive redundant API calls.
9. The original single-device daily report design assumes a single device; when users need multi-device aggregation, the current architecture cannot handle it Solution: The single-stage design (reading dialogue → calling API → generating report) was completely refactored into a two-stage design (Stage 1: export dialogue as JSON per device; Stage 2: merge all exports and call API to generate a summary report). This architectural change was explicitly requested by users.
Key Insight: User requirements change during development. Human users discovered the single-device limitation, while AI did not anticipate it in the initial design. The two-stage architecture is more complex but necessary for real-world use cases. This indicates that human system thinking is superior at anticipating distributed deployment limitations.
10. Scene generation produced zero-friction/gripping bias scenes, despite the injector being enabled (initially only pose_perturb was effective) Solution: The detector only generates specific sub-types of friction/gripping bias ErrorSpecs, which do not trigger during operation. A _augment_specs_with_alternatives() method was implemented to programmatically generate friction/gripping and clamping bias/scrambled specifications when the original detector yields no results. 100 additional friction scenes were generated (55 scrambled, 28 tip overshoot, 17 large offsets), expanding the database to 454 scenes.
Key Insight: Error scene generation is a funnel: detector triggers → ErrorSpec generation → injector application → validation → scene acceptance. Enabling the injector does not guarantee generated scenes—it depends on the frequency of detector triggers. Different error types have distinct acceptance rates depending on the task. In pick-and-place tasks, pose perturbation is more generalizable than friction/gripping anomalies. Programmatic specifications can compensate for the coverage gap of the detector.
11. No MimicGen pre-trained BC-RNN checkpoints are available for PickPlace tasks Solution: A comprehensive search (official repository, HuggingFace, local filesystem) confirmed that MimicGen only provides datasets and not pre-trained model weights. The demo dataset generated by MimicGen is used to design self-training plans via the robomimic framework.
Key Insight: Official releases may provide data but not trained models. Always verify resource availability before planning dependent workflows. When pre-trained checkpoints are unavailable, training from demonstrations becomes a necessary backup solution.
General Issues 12. Model checkpoints are scattered across the filesystem (BC-RNN under tangzijia/, VLA models under zhaoganlong/, total size 47GB), hindering management and reproducibility Solution: Design checkpoints/directories and use symbolic links to avoid duplication: bc_rnn/pick_place → original path, vla/{pi0_libero, pi05_base, pi0_base, pi0_fast_base} → zhaoganlong cache. Updated benchmark_v4.yaml to use the new centralized path.
Key Insight: Large model assets (47GB+ VLA checkpoints) require a symbolic link-based organization to avoid duplication while maintaining centralized discoverability. Scattered checkpoints in the filesystem hinder reproducibility and configuration management.
13. Hugo preamble generation uses hard-coded “AI Daily Summary” and incorrect time zone (+08:00 instead of -05:00), inconsistent with existing bugJournal entries Solution: Adjust the preamble generation to use the correct time zone (-05:00). Solution: The generate_hugo_post() function was modified to extract the actual summary from the double-quote region (line 3, starting with ‘>’) in the report; the time zone was changed to -05:00; time was set to T00:00:00; the “AI Daily Summary” keyword was removed from the keywords.
Key Insight: Code generation should follow existing content standards rather than imposing new ones. Reading the actual report structure (double-quote summary) is easier to maintain than hard-coded strings.
